# Terms and Conditions

## 1. The challenge

The UPAR Challenge at the Real-World Surveillance workshop, WACV 2027, is a
skill-based contest with three independent tracks. These terms cover **Track 3:
Human Pose Estimation**. The challenge is run entirely on Codabench: this
benchmark page is the official source for the task description, data,
evaluation, schedule, rules and announcements.

## 2. Eligibility

- Participation is open to everyone except the organizers and members of their
	research groups.
- You may participate alone or in a team. Each person may belong to one team
	only, and each team may use one Codabench account only.
- To be eligible for ranking and prizes you must register with your real
	identity and affiliation.

## 3. Training data and pre-training

- Models must be trained **only on the training data provided by the
	organizers**.
- The use of external data to fine-tune pose estimation is not permitted.
- Pre-training on COCO and PoseTrack18 is permitted. No other external
	pretraining data or foundation models are allowed.
- **Any use of the test images is prohibited**, including training,
	pseudo-labelling, manual annotation and hyper-parameter selection, and leads
	to disqualification. Test images are never released. Attempts to extract
	them from the evaluation container lead to disqualification.

## 4. Submissions

- Submissions are code submissions as described on the Submission page. The
	submitted code must not access the network or tamper with the evaluation
	environment.
- Submission limits per day and in total are shown on the phase.
- The ranking metric is the mean `AP` across the four hidden subsets, see the
	Evaluation page. The **latest** valid submission of a team counts.
- To win, a submission must outperform the organizers' baseline.

## 5. Verification and publication

- The top-ranked teams must provide their training code and a short
	description of the method (fact sheet) so the organizers can verify the
	result and compliance with these terms. Teams that do not comply are removed
	from the final ranking.
- The top three teams release their code under an OSI-approved open-source
	licence.
- All participants are invited to submit papers to the RWS workshop by Oct 23,
	2026 and to present their work at the workshop.

## 6. Data licence

The UPAR-Pose annotations are published under the Creative Commons
Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 licence. The underlying image
datasets keep their own licences and are for non-commercial research use
only. If you use the data, cite the UPAR paper and the papers of the
sub-datasets.

## 7. General conditions

- The organizers may change the schedule, clarify the rules, or disqualify
	participants who violate these terms or the spirit of the challenge.
- The organizers' decisions on ranking and eligibility are final.
- The data and the platform are provided as is, without warranty.

By registering you accept these terms.

pages.content:
#

Real-World Surveillance: Applications and Challenges, 7th
@ WACV2027
UPAR Challenge Track 3: 2D Human Pose Estimation

## News - Oct 2, 2026: New code & fact sheet submission deadline: **Oct 26, 2026, AoE**. Due to strict WACV deadlines, we must move up the deadline. ## Challenge & Workshop Track 3 of the **UPAR Challenge** at the Real-World Surveillance workshop (RWS), WACV 2027. Everything about this track lives on this Codabench page: task, data, evaluation, submission format, schedule and rules. Announcements go out by email to registered participants. See also the workshop website and Tasks 1 and 2 of the UPAR Challenge. The RWS workshop welcomes both regular submissions on the topic of real-world surveillance and submissions as part of the Challenge: - [RWS Workshop](https://vap.aau.dk/rws/) - [Challenge Task 1: Pedestrian Attribute Recognition](https://www.codabench.org/competitions/18180/) - [Challenge Task 2: Attribute-Based Person Retrieval](https://www.codabench.org/competitions/18196/) - [Challenge Task 3: 2D Human Pose Estimation]() ## The task Top-down 2D human pose estimation on PoseTrack18-format data. For every pedestrian box, predict the **17 PoseTrack18 keypoints** in absolute image coordinates. The submission format keeps 17 keypoint slots for historical PoseTrack18 compatibility. The ear slots stay in the format, but they are not annotated in the ground truth and are ignored by scoring. The challenge builds on the UPAR dataset, which unifies the annotations of several public pedestrian datasets. The test images come from a domain your model has never seen, so the method has to generalise beyond its training data. You submit **code, not predictions**. Your model runs inside the evaluation container on hidden test sets, and only the resulting metrics are published. ## Getting started 1. Read the **Data** page and download the training data and example submission. [Starter Kit](https://github.com/MickaelCormier/UPAR-Challenge-2027-Track3/) 2. Take the **example submission** as your template. It shows the functions the platform calls. 3. Put your model and weights into the submission folder, zip the **contents** of the folder so `run.py` is at the archive root, and upload it under **My Submissions**. See the **Submission** page for the API your `run.py` must expose, and the **Evaluation** page for the metrics. Submissions run in `pytorch/pytorch:2.4.1-cuda12.1-cudnn9-runtime` (Python 3.11, torch 2.4.1, torchvision, numpy, Pillow) with **no network access**. Ship everything your model needs inside the zip. ## Code submission and winner selection After the challenge deadline, participating teams are required to submit their code, models, and a short description of their method (fact sheet) by **Oct 26, 2026, AoE** to **upar.challenge@gmail.com**. A panel of experts will review the entries. The executable/source code should include trained models, training code, and necessary parameters to ensure reproducibility. Teams that do not comply are removed from the final ranking. Note: Submitted codes will not be saved on the evaluation servers. Final submission codebases provided to the organizers will be used only for reproducibility checks and winner verification, and will not be shared publicly or with other participants at any stage. ## Paper submission We strongly encourage all challenge participants to submit a technical paper to the RWS workshop. Your paper should detail your methodology, experiments, and results on the challenge dataset. Accepted papers will be presented at the workshop and published in the WACV workshop proceedings. This is an excellent opportunity to share your insights with the community and gain visibility for your work. Submission Guidelines: - Format: [WACV format](https://wacv.thecvf.com/Conferences/2026/AuthorReviewerGuides) - Submission System: [Openreview](https://openreview.net/group?id=thecvf.com/WACV/2027/Workshop/RWS) - Challenge paper deadline: **Oct 23, 2026, AoE** ## Schedule | Date | Event | | --- | --- | | Sep 30, 2026 | Challenge opens, training data available | | Oct 21, 2026, AoE | Challenge submission deadline | | Oct 23, 2026, AoE | Paper submission deadline | | Oct 26, 2026, AoE | Code & fact sheet submission deadline, code verification starts | | Jan 4/5, 2027 | RWS Workshop at WACV 2027 | ## Citation ```bibtex @inproceedings{specker2023upar, title={UPAR: Unified Pedestrian Attribute Recognition and Person Retrieval}, author={Specker, Andreas and Cormier, Mickael and Beyerer, Jurgen}, booktitle={Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision}, year={2023} } @inproceedings{cormier2023upar, title={UPAR challenge: pedestrian attribute recognition and attribute-based person retrieval-dataset, design, and results}, author={Cormier, Mickael and Specker, Andreas and Jacques, Julio CS and Florin, Lucas and Metzler, J{\"u}rgen and Moeslund, Thomas B and Nasrollahi, Kamal and Escalera, Sergio and Beyerer, J{\"u}rgen}, booktitle={2023 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW)}, pages={166--175}, year={2023}, organization={IEEE} } @inproceedings{cormier2024upar, title={Upar challenge 2024: Pedestrian attribute recognition and attribute-based person retrieval-dataset, design, and results}, author={Cormier, Mickael and Specker, Andreas and Junior, Julio and CS, Jacques and Moritz, Lennart and Metzler, J{\"u}rgen and Moeslund, Thomas B and Nasrollahi, Kamal and Escalera, Sergio and Beyerer, J{\"u}rgen}, booktitle={Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision}, pages={359--367}, year={2024} } ```

pages.title: Data
pages.content:
# Data
## Training data

Training data and starter kit can be found here: [Starter Kit](https://github.com/MickaelCormier/UPAR-Challenge-2027-Track3/)
The use of external data to fine-tune HPE is not permitted.
Pre-training on COCO and PoseTrack18 is allowed. No other external pretraining data or foundation models are allowed.
The hidden test images must never be used for training, pseudo-labeling, or hyper-parameter tuning.


## Keypoints

The submission format keeps 17 keypoint slots for historical PoseTrack18
compatibility. The ear slots stay in the format, but they are not annotated in
the ground truth and are ignored by scoring.

The 17 keypoint slots are listed in this exact order:

```text
 0 nose            1 head_bottom     2 head_top        3 left_ear
 4 right_ear       5 left_shoulder   6 right_shoulder  7 left_elbow
 8 right_elbow     9 left_wrist     10 right_wrist    11 left_hip
12 right_hip      13 left_knee      14 right_knee     15 left_ankle
16 right_ankle
```

## Test data

The test set is hidden. It is mounted into your container, read-only, with this
layout:

```text
input_data/
├── images/
│   ├── 000000397133.jpg
│   └── ...
├── boxes.json      COCO-format: images + person boxes, no pose labels
└── task.json       set name, title, description, protocol, size, keypoint names, skeleton, score prefix
```

`boxes.json` is a normal COCO format.

```json
{
  "images":      [{"id": 397133, "file_name": "000000397133.jpg",
                   "width": 640, "height": 427}],
  "annotations": [{"id": 1219096, "image_id": 397133, "category_id": 1,
                   "bbox": [388.66, 69.92, 109.41, 277.62],
                   "area": 23258.9, "iscrowd": 0}],
  "categories":  [{"id": 1, "name": "person",
                   "keypoints": ["nose", "head_bottom", ...],
                   "skeleton":  [[16, 14], ...]}]
}
```

The `keypoints` and `num_keypoints` fields are **removed** from every
annotation.

You do not have to parse these files yourself: the ingestion script does it
and hands your code one ready-made `sample` dict per image. See the
**Submission** page.

pages.title: Evaluation
pages.content:
# Evaluation

The standard keypoint protocol: average precision over Object Keypoint
Similarity (OKS), `maxDets = 20`.

## Reported metrics

The leaderboard reports the following metrics for each hidden subset, then
averages them across the four subsets.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `AP` | AP @ OKS 0.50:0.95, all areas - **the ranking metric** |
| `AP50` | AP @ OKS 0.50 |
| `AP_medium` / `AP_large` | AP restricted to medium / large people |


The leaderboard ranks by the mean `AP` across the four subsets.

## Detection scores matter

Every prediction carries a `score`. Precision and recall are accumulated in
descending score order, so a model that knows which of its poses are reliable
scores higher than the same model returning a constant. Return a real
confidence if your method has one.

## Ignored ground truth

Following the COCO protocol, annotations with no labelled keypoints and crowd
regions are marked *ignore*: predictions landing there are neither rewarded nor
penalised. They are kept in the reference data precisely so that this
bookkeeping is correct.

## Detailed results

Each scored submission gets a **Detailed Results** page with the full metric
table, a per-keypoint accuracy breakdown, and the inference timing reported
by the ingestion program.

## Reproducing the metric

Scoring uses `pycocotools.cocoeval.COCOeval(iouType='keypoints')` when
`pycocotools` is available. If that import or evaluation path fails, the
scorer falls back to the bundled pure-numpy evaluator instead. The local Docker
image used by this bundle does not include `pycocotools`, so local runs use
the fallback path.

The fallback is a dependency-light reimplementation of the same COCO keypoint
protocol. We checked the fallback against `pycocotools` on the current task
data and the reported scores matched exactly.

The 17-slot output format is kept for historical PoseTrack18 compatibility.
The ear slots stay in the format, but they are not annotated in the ground
truth and are ignored by scoring.

## Ties

Codabench ranks first by the primary leaderboard column, which here is AP at.
If two submissions have the same AP, it keeps sorting left to right across the leaderboard columns, 
so the next tiebreakers are AP50, then AP_medium, then AP_large.

If those are also identical, Codabench finally breaks the tie by submitted_at, with the earlier submission ranked higher.

## Leaderboard

Your **latest** submission is the one shown on the leaderboard, not your best.  
This means only each team’s latest valid submission stays on the leaderboard. 
So for one team, an older better score does not remain visible just because it ranked higher.

pages.title: Submission
pages.content:
# Submission

You upload a zip containing your model, the platform runs it against data you never see.

## The zip

Zip the **contents** of your submission folder, not the folder itself:

```bash
cd my_submission
zip -r ../my_submission.zip . -x "*/__pycache__/*" "*.DS_Store" ".git/*"
unzip -l ../my_submission.zip | head    # run.py must be at the root
```

Required at the root of the archive:

```text
run.py           your entry point
metadata.yaml    copy it unchanged from the example submission
<anything else>  weights, modules, configs
```

## The API

The ingestion program imports `run.py` and calls, once per image:

```python
def predict_image(sample: dict) -> dict | list:
    ...
```

`sample` is:

```python
{
  "image_id":   397133,
  "file_name":  "000000397133.jpg",
  "image_path": "/app/input_data/images/000000397133.jpg",   # absolute, readable
  "width":      640,
  "height":     427,
  "boxes":      [[x, y, w, h], ...],   # COCO xywh person boxes
  "box_ids":    [1219096, ...],        # annotation ids, same order
}
```

Return **one prediction per box, in the same order**, as either

```python
[[[x, y, v], ...17], ...]                      # nested, or a flat list of 51
{"keypoints": [...], "scores": [0.93, ...]}    # with per-person confidence
```

Coordinates are absolute pixels in the full image, not crop-relative. The
ingestion program also accepts numpy arrays and tensors here, as long as they
can be converted to lists. The `score` is used to order detections during
evaluation (see the Evaluation page).


## Runtime environment

- **No network access.** Ship your weights inside the zip. Nothing is downloaded at run time.
- The image is `pytorch/pytorch:2.4.1-cuda12.1-cudnn9-runtime`: Python 3.11,
  torch 2.4.1, torchvision, numpy, Pillow. Anything else your code imports must
  travel in the zip.
- There is a wall-clock limit for the whole run. The ingestion program logs
  per-image timing, and aborts with a readable message rather than a silent
  kill if you run out of budget.
- The working directory is your submission folder, so relative paths to your
  weights work.
